newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin disgraces ex-aide in bid to end intrigues.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin disgraces ex-aide in bid to end intrigues.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin sent a firm warning to Russian officials on Monday to end intrigues and step into line by removing ex-aide Alexander Korzhakov from the military.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky read out an order on Monday, signed by Yeltsin a day earlier, to set moves in motion that will eventually strip the president's shadowy former bodyguard and confidant of his rank as a lieutenant-general.
Korzhakov's disgrace was a punishment for criticising Yeltsin's entourage and threatening to reveal dark secrets about his former allies since his abrupt dismissal as Yeltsin's bodyguard last June.

The move is clearly intended by Yeltsin as a warning to officials that he is ready to get tough with anyone who fights his battles in public or openly seeks more power while he is out of the Kremlin preparing for heart surgery.

"After his sacking on June 20, 1996, Lieutenant-General Alexander Korzhakov has come out with a series of lies concerning the Russian president and members of his family," said the statement read out to reporters by Yastrzhembsky.

"He has allowed himself to publish confidential information he obtained in office. Korzhakov's public threats to disclose information that he possesses are aimed at discrediting top state officials," it said.
Yastrzhembsky said the order was only the start of precedures against Korzhakov. It did not immediately strip him of his rank but that would follow, he said.
It appeared likely that Korzhakov, 46, a career officer in the KGB security service before he became head of Yeltsin's personal security, would now stop being paid by the military.

Korzhakhov's dramatic fall from being one of Russia's most influential figures may still not be complete. He is also fighting allegations that he tried to extort millions of dollars out of a former top businessmen.

Yeltsin's decision to humiliate Korzhakov was partly intended to end speculation about his ability to rule the country from the sanatorium where he is preparing for a heart bypass operation next month.

The disgrace of a man who until recently had access to -- and probably even a say in -- top-level policy-making signalled how seriously the 65-year-old president takes the mudslinging and allegations of sleaze of recent weeks.

Korzhakov rarely emerged from the shadows while in office but he has criticised the most influential people around Yeltsin as he tries to launch his own political career by running for a seat in the lower hosue of parliament.

He has accused Anatoly Chubais, the head of the Kremlin administration, of trying to establish his own "regency" and said Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana Dyachenko has joined forces with Chubais in a powerful team.
An even greater threat to Yeltsin and the Kremlin is the secret knowledge which Korzhakov gained during his years at the president's side and which he has threatened to reveal.

"We (ousted Kremlin officials) are meant to sink into oblivion. This is neither just nor wise because we know very important state secrets," Korzhakov said in an interview published by the German mazgaine Der Spiegel on Monday.
Yeltsin can ill afford to allow the power struggles to disrupt decision- and policy-making which has already been ruptured by his prolonged absence from the Kremlin.

Any more damage to the Kremlin's image would further alienate voters and reduce the chances of Yeltsin's favoured candidates winning regional elections in the coming weeks which could weaken his grip on the upper house of parliament.
